Impact Areas HOT works to solve local challenges that are global in scale and contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Open geospatial data provides government agencies and first responders with critical information to take more informed and locally appropriate action when a disaster or humanitarian crisis hits. Learn More Climate Resilience & Sustainability Open mapping supports strategies to mitigate potential climate impacts, enhance community preparedness, and ensure that communities grow in environmentally sustainable ways. Through mapping climate hazards and realities in the communities, local players can contribute towards finding sustainable solutions by filling in data gaps and contributing to long-term community resilience and development. Learn More Public Health When communities actively participate in mapping their own areas, they create detailed maps that help identify gaps and plan targeted and effective health interventions, ultimately improving the health and well-being of communities globally. Thus, open geospatial data is invaluable for developing policies that address health disparities, enhance equitable health access, and evaluate the effectiveness of public health programs. Learn More Displacement & Safe Migration Conflict, persecution, violence, and natural disasters have caused a record more than 100 million people worldwide to be displaced . Humanitarian organizations and governments require accurate geospatial data to locate and understand the needs of displaced communities, identify potential risks, enable better coordination and resource allocation, and ensure that assistance reaches those who need it most. Learn More Gender Equality By identifying and addressing gender-specific gaps, open geospatial data provides a more nuanced understanding of how resources, services, and vulnerabilities are distributed across different genders within communities, ensuring an inclusive approach and community ownership in the open mapping process. HOT is committed to fostering inclusivity, and by involving women and gender non-conforming people in mapping initiatives, we ensure their needs are prioritized, enabling targeted and effective interventions to promote gender equity and inclusion. Learn More HOT works around the globe to support the use of OpenStreetMap by local communities and help build a local open mapping movement. HOT works across sectors to provide map data that revolutionizes disaster management, reduces risks, and contributes to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Regional Hubs leverage local expertise and resources to create and sustain the open mapping movement. Hubs have a pivotal role in facilitating localized mapping efforts and serve as a vital connection between local communities, NGOs, governments, and international aid organizations, ensuring that mapping initiatives are tailored to regional needs and priorities. Subscribe another address ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists’ signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons OpenAI’s chatbot isn’t just imitating the magazine’s style. It’s also falsely attributing AI-generated images to real artists. Nieman Lab commissioned Brendan Loper to draw a cartoon reflecting on his experience with ChatGPT reproducing his signature. By Andrew Deck Oct. 5, 2026, 4:01 p.m. At the pearly gates, Dolly Parton, in a sparkling gown, stands arm in arm with Tim Curry, dressed as Dr. Frank-N-Furter. “I knew I chose the right plus one,” Parton says to God, who is standing at heaven’s reception desk. That’s the premise of a cartoon that went viral on Twitter in the days after the legendary entertainers’ deaths in late August. One tweet of the cartoon received 25,000 likes, while other versions of the image circulated on Facebook , Instagram , and Bluesky . In the bottom right corner of the cartoon is the pen name “BLOPER,” the signature of New Yorker cartoonist Brendan Loper . But Loper didn’t draw the cartoon, or sign it. It was generated by ChatGPT and first posted to Facebook by a Dolly Parton fan. In the comments section of her post, she wrote she had simply asked ChatGPT to make “a New Yorker-style cartoon.” “I had people writing to me about this cartoon, asking if it was mine,” Loper told me. First came a text from his twin brother, whose friend had seen the AI-generated image. Emails and DMs on social media from strangers followed. “It was very surreal,” he said. A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Brendan Loper’s signature that was posted to Twitter on August 26, 2026 . This wasn’t the first time ChatGPT had reproduced Loper’s signature. In May, a stranger reached out over Instagram to warn Loper that his pen name had appeared in an image output by the chatbot. Over the summer, Loper found additional examples in a Reddit forum about ChatGPT, where users had been posting similar New Yorker-style cartoons they had generated. Loper already knew his work was “out there, getting harvested for all of this [AI] training,” he said. But an image generator faking his signature felt more personal. “I’m not a territorial person, but my name is my name. It felt very much like a violation of my personhood.” RELATED ARTICLE “I don’t want to outsource my brain”: How political cartoonists are bringing AI into their work Andrew Deck June 2, 2025 These days, cartoon signatures are more than a byline. In an era where cartoons are regularly stripped from their original context and circulated on blogs and social media without proper licensing, they can also act as a watermark that ties an illustration to its original creator. “The signature for me is the certificate of authenticity. I only put it on work that I’m putting on the internet that I feel needs to be recognized as from my hand,” Loper told me. “If I put my name on it, it’s official, it’s mine. It really is a brand. It’s the mark that I made.” Loper isn’t the only New Yorker cartoonist whose signature has been reproduced by ChatGPT. In the same online forums are dozens of images with those of other prominent contributors, including Harry Bliss , Emily Flake , Joe Dator , Pat Byrnes , Peter Vey , and Jason Adam Katzenstein . In my own tests, ChatGPT output cartoons with signatures of some of the magazine’s most established cartoonists, past and present, including George Booth , Liza Donnelly , Ellis Rosen , and Saul Steinberg . In all, I documented more than 15 New Yorker cartoonists whose signatures have been used by OpenAI’s image generator without permission or compensation. “We believe the future of creativity is one that is fundamentally human, and our focus is on building tools that empower human creativity and creators,” said a spokesperson for OpenAI in a statement. “We very much appreciate the community flagging bugs and unintended behavior by our models, so we can address them.” After I notified OpenAI of the issue, ChatGPT began to output a new message when I asked it to generate New Yorker-style cartoons: “This prompt may violate our guardrails concerning similarity to third-party content.” Still, as of the publication of this story, it continues to sign some of the generic cartoons it generates with the names of real New Yorker cartoonists. In my tests, ChatGPT regularly generated cartoons with the hallmarks of the 101-year-old magazine’s house style: a black-and-white, single-panel illustration with a sparse background, clean linework, and a sardonic caption — or at least, an approximation of one. Some of ChatGPT’s punch lines don’t make sense. Not every image came with a signature, and some included pen names that were gibberish. But the signatures that did appear were regularly those of real contributors to the magazine, including older cartoonists, like Warren Miller , who published in the 1960s. “I can see the DNA of my work in there, but it still doesn’t look like something I drew,” said Emily Flake, who’s been a New Yorker contributor since 2008. Several ChatGPT-generated cartoons posted online are signed with her pen name, “e. flake.” “It’s kind of like seeing a distant cousin.” The character stances and shading contained echoes of Flake’s visual identity, but she said overall they looked more like amalgamations of several different cartoonists’ illustration styles. Each signature, though, was undeniably hers. “It’s like somebody attributed a quote to me that I didn’t say.” Left: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Emily Flake’s signature that was posted to a Reddit forum in June. Right: A real Emily Flake cartoon published in The New Yorker on August 20, 2026 and licensed via The Cartoon Bank . Top: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Emily Flake’s signature that was posted to a Reddit forum in June. Bottom: A real Emily Flake cartoon published in The New Yorker on August 20, 2026 and licensed via The Cartoon Bank . In 2024, Condé Nast, The New Yorker’s parent company, signed a multi-year licensing deal with OpenAI allowing it to use much of the publisher’s content in its products. The terms of the deal aren’t public, but a spokesperson for The New Yorker told me Condé Nast has never granted an LLM developer permission to train models on its cartoons. Some ChatGPT creations reproduced The New Yorker’s logo alongside cartoons; that is also not allowed in any LLM deals, the spokesperson said. RELATED ARTICLE Hundreds of thousands of videos from news publishers like The New York Times and Vox were used to train AI models Andrew Deck October 30, 2025 OpenAI declined to answer my questions about how its models might have ingested signatures from The New Yorker’s archives during the training process. Even if Condé Nast did want to license cartoons to OpenAI, The New Yorker’s standard cartoonist contract leaves little room for it. The magazine’s two cartoon editors work with a roster of freelancers who submit their work on spec and only get paid if a cartoon is selected for publication. I reviewed several templatized contracts for New Yorker contributing cartoonists, none of which permit licensing for AI training purposes. While The New Yorker has the right to publish commissioned cartoons first, it is not a “work for hire” arrangement and the cartoonist retains ownership of their copyright. So how did OpenAI’s models learn those signatures? It’s possible they were scraped from the internet. Court documents released last month in the ongoing New York Times v. OpenAI lawsuit reveal the extent to which OpenAI knowingly circumvented publishers’ paywalls while developing ChatGPT. Unredacted Microsoft memos described ChatGPT as a “product that destroys its supply chain” and the data scraped to train its underlying LLMs as “the largest theft of labor in human history.” In another memo, Jack Clark, then the policy director of OpenAI, wrote, “[O]ur work on AI and Creativity is going to increasingly lead to us creating systems that substitute for the labor of the people that define the ‘culture’ of society.” (Clark went on to co-found Anthropic.) RELATED ARTICLE “An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI training Sarah Scire September 18, 2026 Many of the cartoonists I spoke to for this story echoed Clark’s sentiment. “It’s an uncanny simulacrum of an impression of a joke,” said Jason Adam Katzenstein , who has been publishing cartoons in The New Yorker since 2014. “But it’s not the point for it to actually be funny or good. The point is that it’s trying to deal a death blow to labor. It’s trying to render individual cartoonists obsolete because we cost money and take time.” Katzenstein was part of the class action lawsuit filed against Anthropic in 2024 by members of the Authors Guild, the largest professional organization for published writers in the United States. Katzenstein’s cartoons had been used in an anthology published by Harper Collins, which was pirated and used by Anthropic to train its Claude models . Last year, a judge ruled that training Claude on the authors’ work was fair use, but that Anthropic’s decision to download and maintain copies of the pirated books was a form of mass copyright infringement. In July, a federal court approved a settlement in the case , granting a $1.5 billion payout to authors and publishers — the largest in the history of U.S. copyright law. Katzenstein considers the reproduction of his signature by ChatGPT to be more than just a violation of intellectual property; to him, it’s closer to false impersonation. “[ChatGPT] is attaching my name to work that I do not endorse or like. It’s slop, and unlike the other slop that I’ve encountered, this is slop that’s pretending to be me.” Several cartoonists I spoke to also differentiated ChatGPT’s ability to mimic their illustration style from the reproduction of their signature. “I’ve had people hack my credit card,” said Joe Dator, a New Yorker contributor for the past 20 years. “That feels like less of a violation than this. When they hacked my credit card, they didn’t dress up like me.” Left: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Pat Byrnes’ signature. Right: A real cartoon by Pat Byrnes from The New Yorker Collection licensed via The Cartoon Bank . Top: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Pat Byrnes’ signature. Bottom: A real cartoon by Pat Byrnes from The New Yorker Collection licensed via The Cartoon Bank . U.S. intellectual property case law has yet to catch up with the rise of AI image generators, but the courts are also likely to treat these issues as distinct. Any copyright infringement claim, for example, would most likely hinge on ChatGPT’s reproduction of each cartoonist’s specific drawing style. “[The signature] is an indication of authenticity, but attribution is a very small part of the fair use inquiry,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. The chief legal challenge in a copyright suit, he said, is that ChatGPT isn’t usually reproducing any specific cartoon in these examples; rather, it’s mimicking a more general style. Other cartoonists have filed copyright lawsuits against companies building AI image generators. One class-action led by the illustrator Sarah Anderson against Stability AI, Deviant Art, and Midjourney has been winding its way through the courts since 2023, but there is no reference to signatures in that filing . RELATED ARTICLE What it takes to sue OpenAI as a journalism nonprofit Andrew Deck June 25, 2025 Alternatively, Grimmelmann says New Yorker cartoonists could have grounds for a “ right of publicity ” case, a body of state-based law that protects individuals from the unauthorized use of their name or identity. For that, there would need to be proof that the AI-generated cartoons were used for a commercial purpose, not just as a joke or gag. While I found no evidence that these AI-generated cartoons are being bought or sold, there are signs that image generators are already displacing the work of professional cartoonists. Last year, The Baltimore Sun fired Kevin Kallaugher , a Pulitzer finalist who had published editorial cartoons in the paper for more than 30 years. And earlier this year, the Sun began regularly publishing AI-generated cartoons in its opinions section. A quick check with OpenAI’s watermark identification tool shows the illustrations were created with OpenAI’s products. “[We] condemn the use of AI for its theft from artists, its misuse of our planet’s resources, and its threat to original, creative thought,” Marc Murphy , the president of The Association of American Editorial Cartoonists, wrote in an open letter published last month. “The Sun is not alone among American newspapers taking this degrading way out.” The New Yorker hasn’t taken any such turn toward publishing AI-generated cartoons, though none of the contributors I spoke to said they could support themselves solely on their commissions from the magazine. A New Yorker cartoon is a calling card, and work for the publication opens doors to commercial work, book illustrations, and other gigs that together make up a livelihood. It is this work that is most threatened by AI, they said. In 1998, Pat Byrnes published his first cartoon in The New Yorker under the pen name “P.Byrnes.” He went on to build a decades-long career with that name. Since he first began drawing cartoons as a teenager, he has always signed it with a period at the end. “It was like signing a letter,” he said. “Here’s my statement — my gift to you to accept or reject.” Across the more than a dozen ChatGPT cartoons I found signed with Byrnes’ name, every one ended with a period. Subscribe another address How publishers are rethinking audience engagement: Five takeaways from the Future of Media Technology Conference “It would be a mistake to try to replicate the creator economy.” By Gretel Kahn Sept. 30, 2026, 3:31 p.m. Earlier this month, just across from the Tate Modern in central London, journalists and media managers gathered for this year’s Future of Media Technology Conference , a one-day event hosted by Press Gazette . Speakers included journalists, technologists, and media professionals like The Economist’s Andrew Palmer, Politico UK’s Katie Palisoul, The Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism’s Mitali Mukherjee, The Logic’s David Skok, and News UK’s Tom Jackson. Here are five takeaways from the event. Publishers are rethinking audience engagement in light of Google Zero RELATED ARTICLE Search traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirely Neel Dhanesha July 22, 2026 RELATED ARTICLE “Affiliation, not just access”: Newsrooms try to move beyond membership to a focus on “belonging” Sarah Ebner May 12, 2026 In the age of declining traffic, publishers are grappling with how to engage and retain audiences. There’s a shift away from volume toward relationship-building, with publishers exploring new ways to measure engagement beyond pure clicks. App downloads, frequency of visits, and newsletter signups were identified as important indicators by The Guardian’s chief support officer, Liz Wynn . “You build motivation, support, effective comprehension of our mission, our purpose, why we exist, why we should keep coming back,” she said. “[It’s a] very important emotional driver, but it’s not enough on its own. We have to focus also on the habit and the value of driving people day to day.” To build those habits, publishers are focusing on community-building, with some even employing AI tools to achieve that goal. Predictive models, such as using AI to recommend users their next read, were cited as a common example of how AI can help drive user engagement. Anna Sbuttoni , deputy head of digital at The Times and The Sunday Times, said her team is now using AI to help with another aspect of audience engagement: comment moderation. “[Content moderation] is still overseen by humans, but it’s just brought that work way down, and it’s freed up that team to now do much more interesting and innovative community-focused work than they were doing when they were just spending hours and hours on this moderation job,” she said. News organizations are training their own in-house creators RELATED ARTICLE News creators get more attention in countries where traditional media struggles Hanaa' Tameez October 28, 2025 Another challenge for news media is increased competition from independent journalists and news creators . This phenomenon has been well-documented in research by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism (RISJ) and was a running thread of discussion across various panels, where legacy media organizations discussed how to adopt creator-led practices while preserving institutional trust, editorial authority and sustainable revenues. The Economist is a prime example of this. The magazine has moved away from its legacy of journalistic anonymity toward putting its journalists’ faces, names, and personalities at the forefront of its value proposition. Its executive editor, Andrew Palmer , said one of the reasons the publication has begun to showcase its journalists is a desire to highlight the humans behind the journalism as AI advances. “It builds a connection, so we definitely have a lot of subscribers who want to see what our journalists do and understand the workings of the newsroom,” said Palmer. Like many newsrooms, The Economist is fostering in-house talent to put in front of the camera as a way to respond to growing audience interest in creators. The team at The Times and The Sunday Times is also thinking about its talent strategy as the next step in audience engagement. Putting journalists in front of the camera is one strategy it is beginning to employ to reach people who might not otherwise engage with the papers. “How can we make people consider getting a Times subscription? A big part of that has been just a complete change in how we approach our social video formats, and that’s really putting our journalists at the front and center of that. Getting people to know the real journalists,” explained Sbuttoni. Earlier this year, The Guardian announced the formation of Guardian Studios — a new creative hub for video-first, personality-led journalism. Leah Green , who leads the initiative, said the team is looking to create a new slate of YouTube shows built around on-screen talent. Green agreed that legacy media has a lot to learn from creators. But news media has one thing that individual creators don’t: brand recognition. “There can be a [certain] panic and [an] overcorrection from legacy brands. There’s so much to learn from the creator economy: personality and how to create fandom,” said Green. “But brand is one thing that an individual creator can never have. It would be a mistake to try to replicate the creator economy.” Jasmine Dawson , senior vice president of BBC Studios, said one of the main things legacy publishers can learn from creators is a deep understanding of their audience. Creators, unlike broadcasters and publishers, “live and breathe” in their audience’s world: They understand them and know what they want. “Obsessing about your audience means not only knowing where they are, but what they want to talk about, what they want to hear from you, what they want to see from you,” she said. Clicks from AI search are starting to become an important metric RELATED ARTICLE Google highlights links from subscribed publications in new AI Overviews update Andrew Deck May 6, 2026 Over the past year, publishers have been reckoning with what many describe as a significant decline in referral traffic, as changes to Google Search reshape how audiences discover news. Google’s rollout of AI Overviews and AI Mode , which provide AI-generated answers directly within search results, has heightened concerns that fewer users will click through to publishers’ websites. “There’s a real tension that exists in terms of what’s happening in partnerships and their relationship with audiences,” said RISJ’s director, Mitali Mukherjee . “We don’t have a clear sign of what exactly will happen.” RELATED ARTICLE Protein grams and retirement plans: Service journalism enters its next era Sarah Ebner September 15, 2026 This uncertainty is one of the main reasons publishers are investing in strengthening direct relationships with their audiences . At the same time, they are examining their relationships with AI companies and their presence in AI search. They want to remain visible across search and AI services while protecting the value of original journalism. The world of AI search was described as the “Wild West,” with the rules of the game still unclear. No one knows exactly what gets to the top of AI search results, for example, making it difficult to build an optimization strategy around a technology with so many unknowns. Tom Jackson , chief technology officer at News UK, underlined the need for news publishers to adapt their content to AI-driven search and discovery, while warning that the field is changing too quickly to make major strategic decisions based on today’s patterns. “One thing I’m finding quite interesting, given my background, is that they’re saying richer metadata may become increasingly important,” said Jackson. “It’s going to be interesting to reopen that tagging and metadata box in this new, agentic AI–focused world.” Despite the uncertainty, publishers still want to experiment with how they can maintain a presence on these platforms. Carly Steven , director of SEO and editorial e-commerce at the Daily Mail, said that, while the publisher’s default position is to protect its IP and focus on creating original content, it has also started experimenting in the AI search space. “We are starting to test a nuanced approach to that…to be more visible on these platforms,” said Steven. “We know our readers are looking for information on these platforms and are starting to look for brands they trust.” Show your value to monetize your content RELATED ARTICLE The Atlantic is getting more subscribers from Google traffic, even as referrals fall Sarah Scire September 16, 2026 What is the monetary value of journalism? And how do we make audiences pay for it? Those questions were at the heart of many discussions. The overwhelming response was that, in order to persuade audiences to pay for news, organizations need to demonstrate the unique value of their journalism. For example, Katie Palisoul from Politico UK explained that the publisher is building better audience data and conversion journeys to demonstrate the value of its paid journalism to users of its free site. By introducing registration for free content, Politico can better understand its audience, identify registered users who are likely to subscribe, and guide them toward premium content. “We are building some foundational elements to be able to show the value of our paid-for content, which is our policy journalism,” she said. The question of monetization extended beyond audiences to conversations around AI, particularly the tension between the short- and long-term economics of allowing AI platforms to use publishers’ content. In the short term, publishers have an incentive to participate in AI platforms — even if the compensation or referral traffic is small — because their content can be relatively fungible. But if every publisher accepts that weaker value exchange, does it undermine the economics of journalism in the long term? Steven from the Daily Mail said that the question of fungibility has never been particularly relevant to the organization, as it strives to create content that is exclusive, original, and not replaceable. “We are really focused on the absolute conviction that our business is valuable, and that that value needs to be paid for,” she said. “We are experimenting, adapting to the landscape as it changes, as new technologies emerge and they become established standards, but fundamentally believe that [our content] has value.” Jackson from News UK framed licensing and deal-making as a core monetization path when it comes to AI, with a strategy that combines partnerships with legal action. This has led the company to strike a deal with Meta while also entering licensing conversations with other AI companies. “Ideally we want to have relationships with all of these people and get fair value back. But if they come in and steal that content, we will sue them,” said Jackson. “It’s not just the monetary value of that deal, which is material. It’s also the ability to then have that close relationship with these organizations.” Newsletters remain valuable for publishers in the age of AI In the midst of such a future-oriented conference, one old piece of technology stood out as a winner across the panels: newsletters. They were framed as direct, differentiated products that deepen reader relationships and reduce reliance on platform algorithms. Many of the news organizations showcased at the conference have invested in newsletters, which remain a strong way to engage directly with audiences and counter declining referral traffic. For The Logic, a Canadian newsroom focused on tech and business, newsletters have been a core part of the organization since the beginning. David Skok , The Logic’s CEO and editor-in-chief, said the publication hasn’t seen a drop-off in open rates, while advertiser performance has continued to grow. He attributes their success to treating the newsletter as a premium, central product of the newsroom. The Logic considers its daily newsletter briefing, which is written specifically by its journalists, the front page of the newspaper. “The way we treat newsletters is really more as their own product,” said Skok. “We were a bit ahead of the curve in that we had this direct relation with our readers, because we just decided very early on that we weren’t going to build our business on the top of some of these algorithms.” Politico Playbook also demonstrates the enduring appeal of newsletters, having spawned numerous global iterations since its launch in 2007. Palisoul from Politico attributed its success to an “obsession with audience”: The team knows exactly who its readers are and what they want from the product. “The Playbook is written with an exact audience in mind: a prime minister, a cabinet minister…But authors think of that person as a person. They don’t think of that person as an MP,” explained Palisoul. “It’s fun. It’s cheeky. It’s got good humor. Great puns. It tells them where they can go for a drink. It’s really focused on the daily life of that individual.” Gretel Kahn is a journalist at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, where this story was originally published . Every 140 minutes.) “Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.” By Philip M. Napoli , Adam Meskouri , Anjini Mani , Grant Socol and Harrison Walley Oct. 8, 2026, 2:38 p.m. In 2025, trust in journalism reached a record low . According to Gallup, only 8% of Republicans expressed trust in the news media, compared with 51% of Democrats. New data show an uptick among Republicans, but overall trust remains near this record low, and the gap between Republicans and Democrats remains substantial. One of the key drivers of this lopsided decline in trust in journalism may be the extent to which news outlets spend time bashing other news outlets, or bashing the news media in general — a phenomenon we call inter-journalism disparagement . Our research team at Duke University’s DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy recently completed a study of the prominence of this phenomenon on each of the “big three” cable news networks (CNN, Fox News, MSNBC/MS NOW); whether it has increased or decreased over time; and whether there are significant differences in the rate of disparagement across networks. The results were stark. Fox News far exceeds the other networks, with inter-journalism disparagement taking place once every 14.5 minutes. In contrast, CNN engages in inter-journalism disparagement roughly every 140 minutes, and MSNBC every 61 minutes. To conduct this analysis, we gathered 15 years of cable news transcripts (2011-2025) for each network. We gathered a random sample of one week’s worth of programming for each year. 1 With this approach, we ended up with 3,543 transcripts and almost 19 million words across the three networks, which equates to roughly 62,000 pages of text. Given the volume of text to be analyzed, we trained OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 to identify attacks against the news media. We developed a 20-page instruction document to help the model code instances of disparagement. GPT-5.5 consistently achieved 99.5% accuracy at identifying inter-journalism disparagement and 100% accuracy for avoiding false negatives, compared to human-coded samples. (You can read more details about the entire training and analytical process here .) We defined inter-journalism disparagement as negative statements about the conduct or content of an explicitly identified journalism target (such as a specific news organization, or the news media in general). Our definition, which is described in greater depth in the full paper, needed to be quite detailed in order for ChatGPT to produce accurate results. Examples of inter-journalism disparagement include: CNN’s Dan Pfeiffer describing “political journalism writ large” as “bad,” “problematic” and “failing massively.” MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow describing The Washington Post’s editorial page as “rabid” and “foaming,” and “super right-wing,” noting: “I can’t believe this is in this real newspaper.” Fox News’ Mark Levin telling viewers that “MSNBC and CNN…have been lying and lying and lying to you for years.” What we found when comparing the three networks tells us a lot about the dynamics of contemporary cable news and partisan journalism. First, Figure 1 shows the rate of journalism disparagement across each of the big three networks. Because the volume of text that we analyzed varies across each network, our primary metric was the rate of disparagement per 1,000 words of transcript text. In this figure, we show not only the rate per 1,000 words, but we also convert that rate into a time-based frequency, using the industry standard of 1,000 words equaling approximately six minutes of air time. In Figure 2, we graph the frequency of inter-journalism disparagement over time. Here, we see that the massive difference between Fox News and CNN/MSNBC persists over the 15-year time period. Still, we do see some dips in the volume of disparagement on Fox News in the two-year periods leading up to the 2016 and 2024 elections, with journalism disparagement levels on Fox News rebounding to near-peak levels in 2025. We haven’t figured out yet what to make of this pattern. CNN and MSNBC seem to converge in their disparagement activity starting around 2017, with MSNBC’s disparagement rate decreasing somewhat, and CNN’s disparagement rate increasing somewhat. This pattern aligns with recent research that has shown, in other contexts, that CNN and MSNBC programming are converging in ways that suggest diminished differences between the more “centrist” CNN and the more left-leaning MSNBC. A key takeaway here is that we should not think about Fox News and MSNBC as flip sides of the same partisan journalism coin. At least in relation to inter-journalism disparagement, these left- and right-leaning cable networks behave very differently. Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming. In order to get a deeper understanding of these differences, we also identified the targets of the disparagement. These results are presented in Figures 3 through 5. Figure 3 presents a breakdown of the most common targets of disparagement on Fox News. By far the most frequent target of disparagement on Fox News is “the media.” Following in a distant second is CNN, with the “mainstream media” rounding out the top three targets. Other relatively frequent targets include The New York Times, MSNBC, and The Washington Post. As should be clear, Fox News devotes far more attention to disparaging journalism as an institution than it does to attacking individual news sources. This stands in stark contrast to what we see when we look at the results for CNN and MSNBC. Looking first at CNN, Figure 4 shows that the network’s most frequent target is Fox News (though with a frequency that wouldn’t crack the top three of the Fox News list). Similarly, as Figure 5 shows, Fox News is also the number one target on MSNBC. Both CNN and MSNBC have the same top three, with Fox News followed by “the media” and the “right-wing media.” These instances of institutional disparagement happen far less frequently on CNN or MSNBC than they do on Fox News. Finally, we were also able to identify which hosts or anchors were the most frequent disparagers of their fellow journalists. Those results can be seen in Figure 6. Given the lopsided amount of inter-journalism disparagement on Fox News, it is not surprising that this graph is dominated by Fox News personalities, with Sean Hannity taking the top spot, followed by Greg Gutfeld and Tucker Carlson (note: our graph for Howard Kurtz reflects his move from CNN to Fox in 2013). This study didn’t distinguish further in terms of the nature of the disparagement across the three networks (for example, in terms of severity or legitimacy). This is something we are exploring in the next stage of this work. Nor did we examine whether viewer exposure to inter-journalism disparagement reduces trust in specific outlets or the institution of journalism. That certainly seems like a reasonable assumption, given the dramatically lower levels of trust in journalism among Republicans that we noted at the outset. We plan to investigate this relationship directly in future research. But what we do see in this research is that disparagement of the institution of journalism, and of particular news outlets, is a much more prominent component of Fox News programming than it is of either CNN or MSNBC. Some researchers have proposed that this kind of high-volume disparagement of news sources that don’t tow the same partisan line takes us beyond traditional notions of partisan journalism and into the realm of “anti-media media.” The goal of anti-media media is to “weaponize the facade of journalism against the roles assigned to journalism” in a democracy. Based on our findings, Fox News fits this characterization. Philip M. Napoli is the James R. Shepley Professor of Public Policy, director of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy, and director of undergraduate studies for the journalism and media minor in the Sanford School of Public Policy at Duke University. Adam Meskouri is a politics researcher at Harvard and Duke. Anjini Mani is an undergraduate at Duke. Grant Socol is a graduate research assistant at Duke. Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke. Rather than analyze the entirety of the networks’ output over this time, we created a “constructed week” for each year, which is a common practice in this kind of content analysis. This involves selecting a random Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc. within each year, so that the sample of programming was reasonably representative of the year as a whole. We included all programming across all dayparts in our constructed weeks. Note: MSNBC was only available through 2023; the network became MS NOW in late 2025. Teresa Mondría Terol of NPR and Bruno Savoca Albors of JPMorgan present at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum at The New York Times Building on September 25, 2026. (Courtesy of Hacks/Hackers) By Andrew Deck Oct. 7, 2026, 3:39 p.m. Late last month, about 150 journalists, researchers, and technologists gathered on the 15th floor of The New York Times Building for a forum on how AI is changing investigative journalism . Just outside the event space was a hallway commemorating the paper’s more than 140 Pulitzer Prize winners, dating back to 1918. One photograph had yet to be hung: a portrait of this year’s winners of the Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting. For one of their winning stories , a team of Times reporters conducted an audit of the SEC’s crypto lawsuits to show weakening enforcement under the second Trump administration. The reporting was assisted by large language models (LLMs). The Times isn’t the only major newsroom using AI tools in major investigations. A record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees this year disclosed AI use to the judges. They used LLMs to organize, summarize, analyze, and translate large document dumps. “At the Times we’re not doing ‘robots tell the news,’ but a number of different [kinds of AI adoption] that can make the work we do more efficient, more effective, and able to do things that otherwise would be very, very hard to do,” said Juliana Castro Varón , the Times’ senior design editor of AI initiatives, in a keynote. Often, “the most useful part [of AI] is the fact that it understands images and understands text, more than creating [them].” RELATED ARTICLE A record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees disclosed AI use this year Andrew Deck August 3, 2026 The Times’ AI Initiatives team, a group of nine journalists and technologists leading AI strategy and deployment in the newsroom, co-hosted the event with Hacks/Hackers , a nonprofit that brings journalists and technologists together to discuss media innovation. (Hacks/Hackers hosted a summit on AI and journalism in Baltimore for the past two years.) The day was packed with workshops, panels, and presentations about the promise of AI for investigative journalism, led by the technology’s most vocal advocates in newsrooms. But the limitations of these tools — including persistent hallucination problems in LLMs, concerns about vibe-coding errors, and budget constraints as AI token costs pile up — were also a common theme. “AI is very good at generating leads, but much less capable of establishing publishable evidence,” said Afrooz Mosallaei , a research associate at the Center for News, Technology & Innovation, during a talk about the nonprofit’s recent report on the topic. “A lot of tasks in an investigation — including verification, source development, textual understanding, and editorial judgment — remain fundamentally human responsibilities.” From search tool to “uber agent” The release of the Epstein Files was a huge moment for AI in investigative journalism . Journalists across the U.S. woke up on January 30, 2026 to a Department of Justice drop of over 3.5 million pages of documents and tens of thousands of images and videos. Duy Nguyen , who leads AI science research at the Times, noted that the PDFs in the Epstein Files would stack as high as the Empire State Building if they were printed out, and would take 11 years for one reporter to read. (Epstein sent an average of 65 emails every day for a decade.) It would take a reporter a month to listen to and watch all the audio and video clips. RELATED ARTICLE AI-powered search is fueling a wave of Epstein Files transparency projects Andrew Deck March 4, 2026 Many newsrooms decided that the early organization and research into these documents was a task primed for AI technologies. Engineers from the Associated Press, NPR, and the Times led a session on how they built tools to help reporters sift through the documents. NPR built an internal search tool that let reporters across the newsroom find the documents relevant to their beats, said Kriti Singh , a design technologist at NPR’s AI Labs. Her team classified documents by type (email, legal filing, flight log, witness list), grouped them by location (city, county, hotel, university), and extracted entities (making sure, for instance, that a search for “Prince Andrew” also surfaced files that mentioned “the Duke of York”). The Times AI Initiatives team built the Epstein Files Engine, an internal chatbot to help reporters comb through the files. “There are so many sorts of threads that you can pull from such a big corpus, and the chat interface really allows [reporters] to dive deep,” said Nguyen. The engine’s interface was built with LibreChat , a free, open-source, self-hosted AI chat platform. A few real prompts from reporters: “Look at our Epstein coverage over the past three months and cross-reference with names of people most mentioned in the documents. Give me a subset of names we haven’t covered as often.” “Find me Kathryn Ruemmler’s email where she said she is missing her ring in Epstein’s apartment.” “Construct a timeline of Epstein’s death, give me a table that I can copy into a spreadsheet. Be very detailed. Surface witnesses, links and quotes where available.” Ultimately, more than 100 Times journalists posed more than 5,000 questions to the engine, and it contributed to at least 20 published stories. “This was a signifier of just how powerful an agentic chat interface could be in a newsroom,” said Nguyen. (His team recently published an academic article detailing the tool’s development.) Since then, the team has created other agentic search tools. Ahead of the Times’ 175th anniversary series , they built “Morgue Bot,” which made it easier for reporters to dive into the Times’ archive. Now, the team is taking chatbots to the newsroom at large. In July, they launched News Agent, which they’re calling the “front door to AI at The New York Times.” The general-purpose internal chatbot plugs into not just the Times’ archives and the Epstein Files, but other databases, internal documents like the Times’ style guide, and the web. News Agent also allows any Times reporter to build their own custom agentic search tool, tailored to a specific project. “It’s an omnibus agent or an uber agent that basically acts as a drop-in replacement for chatbots like Gemini or ChatGPT,” said Nguyen, “but specifically geared to help reporters and editors within the Times newsroom.” The team’s copy for the tool reads, “Ask anything.” Automating the source spreadsheet Any beat reporter will tell you they have a love-hate relationship with their source spreadsheet — that Google Sheet or Excel file that lists the name, title, email address, and phone number of every source they’ve spoken to over the years. Such documents are perfect for remembering the name of a researcher you spoke to five years ago without having to dig through your inbox. But they’re tedious to update. “It can become a dead document that never gets checked,” said J.D. Capelouto , a technology reporter and the newly named AI lead at Semafor. RELATED ARTICLE How The New York Times uses a custom AI tool to track the “manosphere” Andrew Deck February 11, 2026 To try to keep his own source spreadsheet alive and up-to-date, Capelouto made a tool in Google Apps Script , a platform that lets users build small “assistants” within Google Workspace. When he emails someone for the first time, he adds an inbox tag called “New Source.” At the end of each day, the script scans his inbox for any tagged emails, then populates a Google Sheet with all the relevant information about them, including adding a category tag and generating a logline summarizing what they discussed. (There are obvious risks in handling anonymous or sensitive sourcing, but Capelouto said the tool creates minimal new security vulnerabilities since it stays within Google’s ecosystem.) From there, Capelouto started building on top of the spreadsheet. A pop-up sidebar lets him ask who might be a good person to speak with for a story; the tool combs through the spreadsheet and suggests names. Every morning, a script also scans the web for the news of the day on Capelouto’s beat, cross-references those headlines with the source spreadsheet, and sends him an email suggesting a topic to cover and a source to contact. Some of the suggestions aren’t useful, Capelouto admitted, but others have actually prompted him to reach out to someone he’d forgotten about. “A lot of times in journalism, some of the source management work is just saying, ‘Hey, how’s it going?” he said. “This can begin a conversation, then you get a scoop from that.” Philip Bump of Hearst Connecticut Media Group presents at the AI x Investigative Journalism Forum in The New York Times Building on September 25, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Hacks/Hackers) Undercover AI personas Most conversations about AI-generated imagery in investigative journalism revolve around verification . As AI-altered images and deepfakes flood the internet, how do reporters verify the images they come across online, or those sent to them by whistleblowers? The forum didn’t tackle these questions head on, but one presentation highlighted the ways that AI image generators can be harnessed to protect the identity of journalists. Last year, The Markup co-published an investigation into Match Group , the dating app giant that owns Tinder, Hinge, and OkCupid. The nonprofit tech publication owned by CalMatters found that despite an official policy of banning users who are reported for assault, the company failed to keep them off their platforms and hid the scale of the problem from the public. In one case, a Denver cardiologist who was repeatedly accused of drugging and sexually assaulting women he met on Hinge remained active on the platform for three years, even after two different women reported his abuse. (In 2024, he was convicted of crimes against 11 women and sentenced to 158 years to life in prison.) RELATED ARTICLE Can we gamify that? The innovators turning investigations on spying scandals and vote rigging into video games Bhavya Dore August 17, 2026 The Markup’s reporters decided to go undercover. They posed as users on Match-owned apps, then reported themselves from other accounts to see how easy it was to stay on the platform. There was only one problem. “We came across this ethical dilemma: Am I gonna ask my staff or myself to take a photo and put it on the Tinder account?” recalled Sisi Wei , the chief impact officer at The Markup and CalMatters. Even stock photos would subject real people, who had not consented to their likeness being used in the investigation, to reputational harm. Instead, The Markup turned to AI image generators. They found a company that generates visual test imagery and had developed a way to train models without relying too heavily on images of real people. “They look like real human beings, but if you turn on a light switch, you can tell that AI is here,” said Wei. But they were still “real” enough to bypass the dating apps’ content moderation filters. With these new AI headshots and personas in hand, the reporters went back on the apps and created 50 different accounts. Ultimately, their investigation found that even after one of these personas was reported and kicked off a Match-owned dating app, they could get back onto the platforms without changing identifying information. Earlier this year, the 18-month long investigation won a SABEW Award for best technology business reporting . “AI became a way for us to protect our own staff from needing to be a part of the experiment,” said Wei. By Seth C. Lewis and Nick Mathews Oct. 6, 2026, 2 p.m. Editor’s note: Mark Coddington , Seth Lewis , Tamar Wilner , and Nick Mathews write a regular newsletter on recent academic research around journalism. We’re happy to bring each issue to you here at Nieman Lab. Over the past decade, nonprofit news has been seen as one of the bright spots in U.S. journalism — an emblem of hope for the future amid a landscape littered with failures and financial struggles. RELATED ARTICLE Nonprofit news is growing strong — especially local nonprofit news, a new report shows Hanaa' Tameez October 8, 2025 With an average of 10 local newspapers closing each month , joining the thousands that have met that fate already, conditions out there are grim. Largely in response, more than 6,000 nonprofit foundations have made major investments in local news initiatives, totaling some half a billion dollars or more in direct funding for journalism. As a result, the number of U.S. nonprofit news organizations has been growing by double-digit percentages year-over-year. It’s fair to question whether this is sustainable. But in the meantime, at least, what’s not to like about this arrangement — this major push to subsidize local journalism at a time when the for-profit model for it is rapidly vanishing? Behind the scenes, it seems, there are cracks in the foundation, ones that appear to call for greater scrutiny to understand how sustainable and effective this model truly is moving forward. As described in an ethnographic study published recently in Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, Jocelyn McKinnon-Crowley of the University of Memphis spent four months in late 2023 and early 2024 embedded in a four-person nonprofit newsroom in a midsized Rust Belt city, and also interviewed news workers at seven other nonprofit outlets. She focused on the question of labor: What is the impact of this type of journalism on the work and the workers involved? Her main finding is blunt: “The emphasis on funding, on money, and on organizational concerns has become the top priority for individuals working for nonprofit news entities.” And, as journalists “busy themselves” with these administrative chores and organizational imperatives — to keep grant money coming in, to keep funders happy, etc. — it not only comes at the expense of the journalism product but also extracts a heavy toll of unpaid labor from the news workers involved. The situation, McKinnon-Crowley writes, “leads to a double worker exploitation where journalists feel morally obligated to do good work as journalists and to do good work for a morally just (nonprofit) organization.” This exploitation, she says, is perpetuated by the nature of nonprofit reliance, as foundations often “take decision-making power away from journalists and the institution of journalism.” A clear example of this, she says, is the grant-making process, which can require an undue level of administrative burden and can force journalists to put the priorities and interests of funders ahead of those of the community. The result, she contends, is a pernicious cycle: Rather than allowing space for journalists to center the needs of their community, the voices and opinions of the funders are prioritized into perpetuity as nonprofits continually need external funding. This reproduces social inequality, as journalists are incentivized to favor those who can distribute wealth, mirroring similar global trends where the news contributes to making the “information rich get information richer.” Part of the challenge is that, unlike the wall that typically exists between editorial and advertising at for-profit news organizations, there are few clear lines of separation. Funders tend to sit on boards overseeing the news outlets. They shape application forms and set renewal cycles. Journalists interviewed described the “mental formulas they are constantly calculating to keep producing the news.” While such concerns have always been present to some degree — and for-profit news managers, no doubt, are often plenty stressed about their own funding arrangements — McKinnon-Crowley suggests these problems are particularly tough for nonprofit newsrooms given how small and precarious they tend to be, and given how quickly funding provided through one grant cycle can disappear entirely in the next. Even more, the researcher found a distressing level of unpaid work that seemed to be the rule, not the exception, in small-outlet nonprofit journalism. In one example, there was a journalist who officially held titles as executive director and managing editor, though he was not necessarily compensated for such higher-level work. Moreover, that was only the start of his duties required to keep the organization humming. McKinnon-Crowley writes: From what I observed, here is a list of some of his unofficial job duties: fundraiser, party planner, grant writer, mentor, teacher, board member, publisher, figurehead, reporter, editor, tech support, building maintainer, sounding board, community-liaison, coffee-buyer, freelance coordinator, radio personality, podcast scripter, scheduler, photographer, and social media manager. The upshot: Much of the actual work that this person wanted to do as a journalist was, by his own admission, “slipping through the cracks.” McKinnon-Crowley summed it up this way: “As I observed in the newsroom, if you have to return cheese trays from banquets and create fundraising emails, the split priorities lead to gaps in what the organization is able to do.” So, what should be done? McKinnon-Crowley recommends that funders give recurring money without restrictions, fund positions on a longer-term basis (5 to 10 years minimum), help pay for administrative overhead, require less paperwork burden in reporting back, and stop dictating coverage decisions. For nonprofit newsrooms, she says it’s time to start having more conversations about these issues — about what counts as unacceptable interference on the part of funders as well as what the risks are of asking journalists to do too much for too little compensation. In a service-oriented occupation like journalism, working within a “doing good” ethos of a nonprofit only accentuates the likelihood that reporters will treat their jobs like callings, get exploited in the process, and end up burned out and disillusioned (see more on that theme in the roundup below). RELATED ARTICLE A new book looks at how AI is rewiring the newsroom, for better and worse Seth C. Lewis August 6, 2026 “Human versus AI news anchors: A survey study on audience satisfaction and the emotional connection.” By Yuan Ji, in Journalism. China has been one of the world’s leading laboratories for AI news anchors. The experiment began in earnest in 2018, when the Xinhua News Agency introduced a virtual news presenter capable of delivering news around the clock. The pitch was simple: AI could provide a tireless, endlessly replicable alternative to a human anchor. Nearly a decade into that experiment, however, audiences don’t seem ready to trade in the humans. That’s the finding that stands out from a new study of 343 Chinese news consumers by researcher Yuan Ji. The study examined how audiences perceive AI anchors, including their engagement, emotional connection, and satisfaction compared with human anchors. The numbers tell a fairly clear story. Only 4.96% of respondents said they found AI anchors very engaging. Another 25.07% said they were somewhat engaging. So nearly three-quarters of respondents did not describe AI anchors as engaging in either of those ways. The satisfaction gap is even more pronounced. Just 5.25% said they were more satisfied with AI anchors than with human anchors. Another 24.78% said they were equally satisfied. That means roughly seven in 10 respondents did not report being equally or more satisfied with AI anchors. For news organizations, the finding raises an important question: What happens when technology solves a problem that audiences don’t necessarily think needs solving? AI anchors offer obvious efficiencies. They can work continuously, be reproduced across broadcasts and locations, and potentially reduce the costs associated with producing and presenting routine news. But those advantages matter less if audiences don’t find the result engaging or satisfying. That’s an important consideration for journalists as AI moves deeper into news production . The technology is getting better at mimicking the mechanics of journalism. But journalism is more than mechanics. As Yuan Ji found, audiences also respond to the people delivering the news — and to the sense of connection, credibility, and human presence those people provide. The finding doesn’t mean AI won’t change journalism. It does suggest that news organizations should think beyond what AI can do and consider what audiences actually value . Efficiency may be one reason to use an AI anchor, but efficiency alone doesn’t guarantee engagement or satisfaction. For now, the numbers offer some good news for human journalists in television. AI may be ready for the news desk, but audiences, at least for now, still seem to want a person sitting behind it. RELATED ARTICLE In Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deserving Sarah Scire May 8, 2020 “Government-funded watchdog journalism? Analyzing Canadian media workers’ self-perceptions of independence under the local journalism initiative.” By Chris Arsenault, in Journalism Practice. Government funding might seem like an obvious threat to journalistic independence. But Canadian journalists who receive public money say it hasn’t interfered with their work. Instead, many still point to advertisers as the bigger threat. This new study explores the journalists working under Canada’s Local Journalism Initiative , a federal program that has provided more than $128 million since 2019 to support hundreds of reporting positions at news organizations across the country. Researcher Chris Arsenault interviewed 22 journalists whose positions are supported by the program. What they said complicates the familiar concern in journalism, that accepting government money inevitably makes it harder for reporters to hold power to account. The journalists certainly recognized the optics. Many worried that government funding could make audiences question their independence or create the appearance of a conflict. But none said the funding had actually changed what they could report. None could point to a story they had avoided or softened because of the government support. And none could identify a source who had treated them differently because their salary was publicly funded. When journalists described actual threats to their independence, they were more likely to talk about advertisers. Several reporters recalled situations in which advertisers had made it more difficult to scrutinize local businesses, organizations or other powerful figures. For these journalists, commercial pressure wasn’t an abstract concern about appearances — it was something they had experienced in their newsrooms. That distinction is worth considering in an industry where the traditional business model has collapsed in many local communities. Journalists may understandably worry about accepting money from the government. But if the alternative is a newsroom with fewer reporters, fewer resources, and greater dependence on advertisers, public funding may sometimes give journalists more room to do independent reporting, not less. The journalists weren’t convinced the funding program could fix the larger financial problems facing local news, however. Many saw it as temporary help rather than a long-term solution. The findings suggest journalists may need to think differently about where threats to independence actually come from — whether from a dependence on government or advertising or some other source. Public funding may not eliminate the challenges facing local journalism, but it seems positioned to give reporters the resources and freedom to do work that commercial pressures have sometimes made harder. “‘This is how journalism has always been done’: White neutrality, newsroom norms, and an AI intervention in source diversification.” By Gavin Adamson, Asmaa Malik, Shari Okeke, and Jisele Bailey-Hay, in Journalism. Adding AI to the newsroom does not necessarily help journalists find better sources in the moment. In a new study of Canadian journalists, the technology was more useful as a mirror, helping reporters look back at their coverage and see whose voices they routinely include — and whose they don’t. Researchers interviewed 12 journalists at a mid-sized Canadian daily and demonstrated an AI tool designed to track the types of sources appearing in news stories. The tool categorizes sources into groups such as politicians, authorities, experts, organizations, and people speaking from personal experience. The journalists generally supported more inclusive sourcing. They saw it as important to accurate, fair and accountable journalism. But they also described why it can be difficult to put that ideal into practice. Time pressure, unsurprisingly, was a major obstacle. Reporters working on deadline often turn to sources they know they can reach quickly, including government officials, police, academic experts, and other institutional voices. Finding people outside those established networks takes time, particularly in newsrooms that have fewer reporters and less time for relationship-building. The result can be a heavy reliance on white and official sources, with the same voices and institutions appearing repeatedly in the news even when journalists recognize that their coverage would benefit from a broader range of perspectives. In this study, the AI tool was found to do little to change that during the reporting process. The journalists did not envision using it to tell them whom to call for a story or to help them find a source before deadline. Instead, they saw value in using it afterward, reviewing individual stories or larger collections of coverage to identify patterns in their sourcing. That makes the technology less of a reporting assistant and more of a feedback mechanism. It could help a reporter or editor notice, for example, how often official sources appear in their coverage or how rarely people with direct experience of an issue are quoted. That kind of reflection could matter if newsrooms use it as part of their regular editorial conversations. The technology can make patterns visible that are otherwise easy to overlook amid the daily rush of producing the news. But seeing a problem is not the same as fixing it. An AI system can identify who appeared in a story. It cannot build relationships with communities, earn the trust of unfamiliar sources, or give reporters more time to do the work. Overall, AI can help newsrooms see their sourcing habits more clearly, but it cannot, at present, create the conditions necessary to change them. If source diversity is going to become a sustained part of journalism, it will require newsroom expectations and resources to support it, not simply another piece of technology. “Stuck between democracy and a layoff: Connecting journalists’ personal disillusionment to overall normative press evaluations.” By Alexis Haskell, in Journalism Practice. Many journalists enter the profession believing they can make a difference. They expect to inform the public, explain complicated issues, give people a voice, and contribute to democracy. This new study suggests that when those expectations collide with the realities of working in journalism, journalists can become disillusioned with more than their own jobs. Alexis Haskell surveyed 695 U.S. journalists and found that disillusionment is a measurable experience among American journalists. The concept is different from burnout, the researcher argues. Burnout describes exhaustion and being overwhelmed by work. Disillusionment describes a deeper break between what journalists expected their careers to be and what they actually experienced. On average, the journalists surveyed were more disillusioned than not. Haskell measured the concept through their feelings about their work, their expectations for the profession and their sense of purpose. That disillusionment was also reflected in how journalists viewed journalism as a whole. Those who were more disillusioned were more likely to give the press lower marks for five of six democratic roles examined by the study. They were less positive about journalism’s ability to inform, analyze, provide a forum for public discussion, foster social empathy, and mobilize audiences. The strongest relationships were found in analysis and the public forum. More disillusioned journalists were particularly likely to believe the press was failing to help people understand complicated issues or provide space for public conversation. There was one exception: Disillusionment was not related to journalists’ evaluations of investigative journalism. Haskell suggests that investigative work may occupy a different place in journalism’s professional culture. It is highly prestigious, frequently celebrated through major awards and often associated with individual achievement. The other roles are more directly tied to journalism’s service to audiences and communities. That difference gets at what makes disillusionment important. Journalists who are disillusioned aren’t necessarily saying they can no longer do good journalism. They may instead be questioning whether journalism, as a profession, is accomplishing what they believed it was supposed to accomplish. The finding connects the personal experience of working in journalism with a broader assessment of the field. When journalists encounter low wages, layoffs, shrinking staffs, and other pressures, the consequences may extend beyond their own careers. They may begin to lose faith not just in the job, but in journalism’s ability to fulfill the public purpose that drew them to it in the first place. A previous version of this piece stated that 550 nonprofit newsrooms operate in the U.S. This is inaccurate and it is difficult to estimate the number of nonprofit newsrooms in the country.
